entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12787"/><div sID="gen23728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12787"/><hi type="bold">5. what Balak ... consulted--</hi>how Balak plotted to destroy thee by getting Balaam to curse thee (<reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Nu 22:5</reference>).<div eID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what Balaam ... answered--</hi>how the avaricious prophet was constrained against his own will, to bless Israel whom he had desired to curse for the sake of Balak's reward (<reference osisRef="Num.24.9-Num.24.11">Nu 24:9-11</reference>) [Maurer]. Grotius explains it, "how Balaam answered, that the only way to injure thee was by tempting thee to idolatry and whoredom" (<reference osisRef="Num.31.16">Nu 31:16</reference>). The mention of "Shittim" agrees with this: as it was the scene of Israel's sin (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.5">Nu 25:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2Pe 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Re 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Shittim unto Gilgal--</hi>not that Balaam accompanied Israel from Shittim to Gilgal: for he was slain in Midian (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Nu 31:8</reference>). But the clause, "from Shittim," alone applies to Balaam. "Remember" God's kindnesses "from Shittim," the scene of Balaam's wicked counsel taking effect in Israel's sin, whereby Israel merited utter destruction but for God's sparing mercy, "to Gilgal," the place of Israel's first encampment in the promised land between Jericho and Jordan, where God renewed the covenant with Israel by circumcision (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.2-Josh.5.11">Jos 5:2-11</reference>).<div eID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know the righteousness--</hi>Recognize that, so far from God having treated thee harshly (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mi 6:3</reference>), His dealings have been kindness itself (so "righteous acts" for gracious, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.11">Jud 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">112:9</reference>). <div eID="gen23731" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12790"/><div sID="gen23738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12790"/><hi type="bold">8. He--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath showed thee--</hi>long ago, so that thou needest not ask the question as if thou hadst never heard (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mi 6:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">De 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.11-Deut.30.14">30:11-14</reference>).<div eID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what is good--</hi>"the good things to come" under Messiah, of which "the law had the shadow." The Mosaic sacrifices were but suggestive foreshadowings of His better sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">He 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">10:1</reference>). To have this "good" first "showed," or revealed by the Spirit, is the only basis for the superstructure of the moral requirements which follow. Thus the way was prepared for the Gospel. The banishment of the Jews from Palestine is designed to preclude the possibility of their looking to the Mosaic rites for redemption, and shuts them up to Messiah.<div eID="gen23740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justly ... mercy--</hi>preferred by God to sacrifices. For the latter being positive ordinances, are only means designed with a view to the former, which being moral duties are the ends, and of everlasting obligation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.6">12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Am 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.24">24</reference>). Two duties towards man are specified--justice, or strict equity; and mercy, or a kindly abatement of what we might justly demand, and a hearty desire to do good to others.<div eID="gen23741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to walk humbly with thy God--</hi>passive and active obedience towards God. The three moral duties here are summed up by our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mt 23:23</reference>), "judgment, mercy, and faith" (in <reference osisRef="Luke.11.42">Lu 11:42</reference>, "the love of God"). Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jas 1:27</reference>. To walk with God implies constant prayer and watchfulness, familiar yet "humble" converse with God (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Ge 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">17:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23742" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12791"/><div sID="gen23743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12791"/><hi type="bold">9. unto the city--</hi>Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man of wisdom--</hi>As in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.6">Pr 13:6</reference>, Hebrew, "sin" is used for "a man of sin," and in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Psa 109:4</reference>, "prayer" for "a man of prayer"; so here "wisdom" for "the man of wisdom."<div eID="gen23744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall see thy name--</hi>shall regard Thee, in Thy revelations of Thyself. Compare the end of <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>. God's "name" expresses the sum-total of His revealed attributes. Contrast with this <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Is 26:10</reference>, "will not behold the majesty of the Lord." Another reading is adopted by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate, "there is deliverance for those who fear Thy name." English Version is better suited to the connection; and the rarity of the Hebrew expression, as compared with the frequency of that in the other reading, makes it less likely to be an interpolation.<div eID="gen23745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hear ... the rod, &c.--</hi>Hear what punishment (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mi 6:13</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">24</reference>) awaits you, and from whom. I am but a man, and so ye may disregard me; but remember my message is not mine, but God's. Hear the rod when it is come, and you feel its smart. Hear what counsels, what cautions it speaks.<div eID="gen23746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.47.7">Jr 47:7</reference>). <div eID="gen23747" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12793"/><div sID="gen23750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12793"/><hi type="bold">11. Shall I count them pure--</hi>literally, "Shall I be pure with?" &c. With the pure God shows Himself pure; but with the froward God shows Himself froward (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>). Men often are changeable in their judgments. But God, in the case of the impure who use "wicked balances," cannot be pure, that is, cannot deal with them as He would with the pure. Vatablus and Henderson make the "I" to be "any one"; "Can I (that is, one) be innocent with wicked balances?" But as "I," in <reference osisRef="Mic.6.13">Mi 6:13</reference>, refers to Jehovah, it must refer to Him also here.<div eID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bag--</hi>in which weights used to be carried, as well as money (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.13">De 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pr 16:11</reference>). <div eID="gen23751" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12796"/><div sID="gen23755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12796"/><hi type="bold">14. eat ... not be satisfied--</hi>fulfiling the threat, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">Le 26:26</reference>.<div eID="gen23755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee--</hi>Thou shalt be cast down, not merely on My borders, but in the midst of thee, thy metropolis and temple being overthrown [Tirinus]. Even though there should be no enemy, yet thou shalt be consumed with intestine evils [Calvin]. Maurer translates as from an Arabic root, "there shall be emptiness in thy belly." Similarly Grotius, "there shall be a sinking of thy belly (once filled with food), through hunger." This suits the parallelism to the first clause. But English Version maintains the parallelism sufficiently. The casting down in the midst of the land, including the failure of food, through the invasion thus answering to, "Thou shalt eat, and not be satisfied."<div eID="gen23756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt take hold, but ... not deliver--</hi>Thou shalt take hold (with thine arms), in order to save [Calvin] thy wives, children and goods. Maurer, from a different root, translates, "thou shalt remove them," in order to save them from the foe. But thou shalt fail in the attempt to deliver them (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">Jr 50:37</reference>).<div eID="gen23757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which thou deliverest--</hi>If haply thou dost rescue aught, it will be for a time: I will give it up to the foe's sword. <div eID="gen23758" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 16. statutes of Omri-- the founder of Samaria and of Ahab's wicked house; and a supporter of Jeroboam's superstitions ( 1Ki 16:16-28 ). This verse is a recapitulation of what was more fully stated before, Judah's sin and consequent punishment. Judah, though at variance with Israel on all things else, imitated her impiety. works of ... Ahab-- ( 1Ki 21:25 , 26 ). ye walk in their counsels-- Though these superstitions were the fruit of their king's "counsels" as a master stroke of state policy, yet these pretexts were no excuse for setting at naught the counsels and will of God. that I should make thee a desolation-- Thy conduct is framed so, as if it was thy set purpose "that I should make thee a desolation." inhabitants thereof-- namely, of Jerusalem. hissing-- ( La 2:15 ). the reproach of my people-- The very thing ye boast of, namely, that ye are "My people," will only increase the severity of your punishment. The greater My grace to you, the greater shall be your punishment for having despised it, Your being God's people in name, while walking in His love, was an honor; but now the name, without the reality, is only a "reproach" to you.
